# pqscan

A small, fast, chainable TLS / QUIC cipher-configuration and post-quantum
readiness scanner. One static binary that enumerates protocol versions,
cipher suites, key-exchange groups, signature algorithms and certificate
properties — scores every observation on a PQC-readiness rubric — and
speaks the Project Discovery dialect (stdin → stdout, streaming JSONL).

**Status:** pre-alpha. The canonical specification lives at
[`docs/spec.md`](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md);
the M0 measurement gate ([PQ-01 register](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/issues/4))
is in progress.

## What it does

- **[fast](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#5-feature-set)** — one engineered handshake per target: negotiated parameters, certificate chain, ALPN, features.
- **deep** — exhaustive suite-by-suite, version-by-version, group and signature-algorithm probing (offer-one / observe-accept), HRR detection, resumption and 0-RTT checks.
- **pq** — forced-group PQ ladder, PQ signature and certificate classification, estate-wide readiness verdicts with an HNDL risk flag.
- **Two planes** — TCP (crypto/tls + uTLS) and QUIC (quic-go) on UDP/443; HTTP/1.1 + h2 via ALPN, h3 via direct QUIC handshake.

## Quick start

```bash
subfinder -d example.com -silent | pqscan -mode fast -jsonl -o assets.jsonl
```

```bash
naabu -l domains.txt -p 443,8443,993 -silent | pqscan -from-naabu -mode fast -jsonl
```

## Prior art — what pqscan learned from

The cipher-configuration space is well-trodden; pqscan exists because the
existing tools each stop one step short of the intersection this project
needs. Credit where the ideas came from, honestly recorded:

| Tool | What pqscan learned from it | Where it stops short for this project |
|---|---|---|
| [cryptonice](https://github.com/F5-Labs/cryptonice) | The scan-menu model (TLS + HTTP + DNS + fingerprint in one report) and the readable-JSON reporting shape | Python's per-target loop doesn't reach the throughput this contract wants, and PQC groups/signatures sit outside its view |
| [gnutls-cli-debug](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/gnutls-cli-debug.1.html) | The gold standard of exhaustive probing: version-by-version, suite-by-suite, offer-and-observe | One interactive target at a time; groups and signatures aren't scriptable as a matrix |
| [testssl.sh](https://github.com/testssl/testssl.sh) | Broad protocol coverage, including legacy versions, in one portable file | Shell's ceiling on concurrency makes estate-scale runs impractical; PQC handling stays opaque |
| [sslyze](https://github.com/nabla-c0d3/sslyze) | A clean probing library design that many Python scanners (incl. cryptonice) build on | Same per-target serialism; no pipe-first output |
| [zgrab2](https://github.com/zmap/zgrab2) | The scale architecture: modular scanners measured in handshakes/s, feeding zmap | One-or-few handshakes per host by design — the depth (suite/group ladder) is the missing altitude |
| [masscan / zmap](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan) | Proof that disciplined rates make internet-scale port discovery possible | They are port scanners, deliberately; they feed pqscan rather than doing its job |
| [TLS-Scanner](https://github.com/tls-attacker/TLS-Scanner) | Research-grade exhaustive protocol analysis done right | Academic packaging; not an ops-chain citizen |
| [httpx / nuclei / naabu](https://github.com/projectdiscovery) | The dialect this tool speaks: pipe-first input, streaming JSONL, silent output, resume, shard | Their focus is HTTP content, not the cipher-configuration plane — a deliberate division of labour |
| [Censys / Shodan](https://search.censys.io) | The value of PQ observations at scale | Remote datasets cannot probe your target list or a new IP range on demand |

The synthesis: port and host discovery stay with the neighbours
([compose, don't rebuild](recipes.qmd)); pqscan owns the
cipher-configuration plane — TLS + QUIC handshake parameters, certificates
and PQC classification — at chain-compatible speeds.
